Maladaptive Strategies.value: constantly scan environment for signs of threat

Threat.value: I notice potential weapons or dangerous objects in any environment
Being superalert or watchful or on guard
My body reacts to danger before I have even had time to think

Memory.value: My memories of the event come in disconnected pieces that do not fit together
Remembering the event brings back the same terror I felt at the time
Remembering what happened during the frightening event is just like looking at photographs of it in my mind.

Negative Appraisals.value: I have permanently changed for the worse
You can never know who will harm you
I am permanently an outsider now

issues.item: Restrict Eating: control eating strictly to feel in control
issues.explanation: Restricting eating to feel in control is not well supported by the rest of the profile. The other endorsed items center on partner-violence-related threat monitoring, hypervigilance, sensory memory, and danger appraisals. In contrast, restrictive eating reflects a different coping theme that is not echoed elsewhere in Threat, Memory, or Negative Appraisals, and it sits awkwardly with the formulation in which Maladaptive Strategies feed Threat. Scanning surroundings and mirror checking plausibly amplify threat, but strict eating control does not connect clearly to the described trauma pattern.

vignette: Priya, a 48-year-old South-Eastern Asian tutor, spent the first years of her marriage with a quiet affection that soon turned violent. The night she remembered most clearly, her husband had slammed a heavy glass cup into her hand, shattering it into splinters. He shouted and slammed his fist against the wall, the impact echoing in the small apartment where Priya had only recently moved in with him. When he had walked away, her heart pounding, she was left with a fractured sense of safety and a series of disjointed images that flashed only in brief, harsh bursts- the cracked glass, the shaking floor, the sudden scream. That memory, though fleeting, has since dominated her perception of the world, and it is the very foundation of the terror she carries today. The self-deprecating belief that she was "permanently changed for the worse" has only intensified the splintered recollections. Priya often tells herself that she is a damaged shell, an outsider in a society that expects her to be unscathed. This appraisal of a ruined self has amplified the sharpness of the memories, turning each fragment into a living echo that can be triggered at a moment's notice. When a quiet hallway, a quiet hallway, suddenly feels too quiet, she can recall the night's violence with vivid clarity, and the same terror that gripped her then washes over her now. The weight of those negative thoughts has made the past feel all too present, and the past continues to weigh heavily on her. The fragmented memory of that night also feeds into the compulsive strategies that now dominate her day. Every morning before she leaves the house to tutor children, Priya scans her surroundings: the kitchen light switch, the coat hanging on the back of the chair, the shape of the door handle. When she sees a mirror-whether it be a framed picture or a reflective surface on a car-she is compelled to stare back at herself, to confirm that she looks safe, that no threat is lurking in her own reflection. These checking rituals are the only means by which she feels she can assert control over a reality that feels constantly ready to betray her. The compulsion to check has become so ingrained that Priya now finds herself unable to leave the house without first double-checking that no one is watching, that no one will follow her into the quiet street. She knows she should not be so worried, yet the belief that danger could always emerge keeps her in a state of relentless vigilance. This constant vigilance feeds the threat perception that colors her entire environment. Priya reports that even in the presence of a familiar child's laughter, she can't help but pause, searching for hidden weapons or menacing figures. She reports that her body reacts before her mind can catch up- a racing pulse, a tightening in her chest, an involuntary gasp when a stranger glances at her. The awareness that every object or face could be a weapon or threat reinforces the memory of the night she was struck. In turn, the vivid recollections of that night make the environment feel like a battlefield. The cycle is closed: her negative appraisal of being a damaged outsider drives her memory to become more traumatic; that memory forces her into maladaptive checking, which heightens her sense of threat; the perceived threat sharpens her memory, which keeps her trapped in this loop. Over the past five years, Priya's coping behaviors have begun to interfere with her occupation. While she once taught students with confidence, she now misses appointments because she can't find a clear way out of a crowded hallway without feeling the urge to check each step. She feels increasingly alienated from her students, who sometimes notice her hurriedness and her nervous glances at the windows. Her marriage has deteriorated further: she no longer speaks to her husband about her fears, fearing that she might be dismissed as paranoid. At home, she keeps a safe space-a small corner of the living room with a sturdy chair and a locked box-where she can retreat when the memories flood back. Yet even there, she cannot fully silence the sense that someone is watching from outside the window. The moment that finally pushed Priya to seek therapy was a near-miss on the street. She was walking home from an evening tutoring session when a car door opened unexpectedly. A shadowy figure stepped out, and for a fleeting instant, Priya felt as if the car's door itself could be a weapon. The instant she saw the figure step aside, she realized she could have been harmed. The panic that followed was unbearable, and she returned home shaking, knowing that the thought of another threat was inevitable. The thought that she would continue living in such a state, unable to trust her own body or mind, made her desperate to break the cycle. Priya now hopes to reclaim a sense of safety and to restore her confidence in her own memories, so that she can once again engage with the world without the constant, paralyzing dread that has kept her in a perpetual state of watchfulness.
